reviews.author: manul garlic
reviews.text:
El Senor Dulce means ‘sweet gentleman’ in Spanish. This place, opened by CEO Won-yong Park in 2015, is said to be a place where CEO Park’s life is intact. In 1987, he was taken by his parents to Argentina. He lived as an immigrant for 10 years and gained a variety of experiences, including working at Korean restaurants and clothing stores. Afterwards, he traveled to famous wine regions around the country and gained a variety of wine experiences. After returning to Korea during the 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup, he obtained culinary qualifications in Korean and Japanese cuisine, worked as a manager at a restaurant, and decided to use his experience in Argentina to open a wine bar where he could enjoy wine comfortably. The first wine bar opened in Garosu-gil, Sinsa-dong, ‘Dulce y suave (Sweet and Soft)’ was opened like that. Before Garosu-gil was built, a wine bar located in a quiet residential area was in business for 10 years. It's a place I really liked too. The second wine bar is ‘El Señor Dulce’. CEO Park’s management philosophy is to use good ingredients. #Jamon played a part in making this place famous. Jamon Iberico Bellota from ‘Cinco Jotas,’ the highest-quality jamon brand supplied to the Spanish royal family, is served with Sicilian olives.  It is made from the hind legs of 16-18 month old Iberico black pigs, pickled in sea salt and aged for 36 months. An unexpected match was the Pruneti extra virgin olive oil that came with the jamon. It's been a while since I enjoyed drinking wine.
.
.

reviews.author: Because he’s a genius
reviews.text:
‘Le Chamber’, located in the middle of Cheongdam-dong, just looking at its location makes you realize that considering cost-effectiveness is not very meaningful.
In fact, the admission fee of 10,000 won is a bit burdensome, but when you actually visit, the atmosphere and cocktail quality are so great that you think, ‘But it’s worth it.’
Personally, I had a great time here thanks to a “very grateful person,” and because of the importance of the place, I feel like I want to go again in the future, even if I had to pay my own money.
However, as expected, I feel less anxious if I am accompanied by a ‘very grateful person.’

The cocktail itself was so good that I couldn't help but exclaim, "This was really well made," even when I was already a bit drunk.
In particular, the cocktail that came in a paper bag was a masterpiece with a combination of cinnamon and smoke flavor, making it almost impossible to feel the harshness of alcohol.
Maybe that's why, even though I don't usually enjoy cocktails and snacks together, I kept reaching for this place and was slightly shocked by the swelling in my face the next day.

What is disappointing is the subtle lack of professionalism in the service department.
When asked for a cocktail recommendation, if you explain, ‘I like this style,’ you usually get a wide range of suggestions, but here, the explanation was a bit unkind and the range of recommendations was narrow.
I could have been more impressed thanks to the atmosphere and the quality of the cocktails, but I feel like this part left a slight flaw.

Nevertheless, thanks to its special location in Cheongdam-dong, stylish interior, and great cocktails, it is a place worth visiting if you want to have a drink at a proper bar once in a while.
However, if the steep price tag along with the entrance fee is burdensome, it may not be easy to go as often as you think, so I recommend going for anniversaries or important appointments.

reviews.text: It is a complex cultural space of the Songeun Cultural Foundation, registered as a foundation under the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism. It was built by Herzog & de Meuron, headquartered in Basel, Switzerland, and is a beautiful building that has become a new landmark in Cheongdam-dong. There is an exhibition space on the 2nd and 3rd floors and the second basement level, and currently a solo exhibition by Swedish artist duo Nathalie Djurberg and Hans Berg is being held. Animation videos, sculptures, and installation works were placed in various spaces, and in particular, the work connecting from the ground to the second basement level was an incredible work that was difficult to see anywhere else. It is scheduled until July 13th, so I highly recommend watching it.

reviews.author: un promeneur solitaire
reviews.text:
Natalie Duberg and Hans Berg attracted attention by presenting works that attractively combined visual art, music, and 3D storytelling based on collaboration. Natalie Duberg, born in Lücésil, Sweden in 1978, has gained fame for her suggestive and metaphorical animations using clay and charcoal, and her partner Hans Berg, born in Retvik, Sweden in 1978, is in charge of producing music that harmonizes with Duberg's visual narratives. Natalie Duberg and Hans Berg, who have been collaborating as a duo since 2004, transcend the boundaries of traditional art and weave immersive stories across animation, music, sculpture, and installation.

Natalie Duberg began her career at the Malmö Art Academy, where she fell in love with storytelling and narrative. Duberg's early work, influenced by various motifs such as fairy tales, folklore, and mythology, became a solid foundation for the fantastical world that she and Hans Berg would later create together. Hans Berg's electronic music adds the dimension of sound to Natalie Duberg's animation work and allows viewers to become even more immersed in the vivid, breathing story.
Clay charcoal animation implemented using ‘stop motion’, a film technique that divides and shoots each frame to create the illusion that the object is moving, is treated as their main work. By incorporating three-dimensional installations and sculptures to create an exhibition environment that requires physical and sensory intervention from visitors, the eerie and enchanting narrative is maximized.

Duberg and Berg's work is reminiscent of the films of Tim Burton and the Quay brothers, evoking both nostalgia and melancholy whimsy. The duo follows the playful language of classic comics by expressing the characters' facial expressions in exaggerated and distorted ways. As the narrative unfolds, the subtle balance between purity and decadence becomes exquisitely balanced. This is similar to the narrative unique to early Disney animation, which exceptionally evokes emotional sympathy from viewers, and can also be associated with the fantastical images seen in the surrealist and expressionist trends.

Their works also show the satire of 18th- and 19th-century caricatures, which are rooted in ghost stories that were widespread in central and northern Europe between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. The surreal depictions of fantasy creatures and hell by the 15th-century Dutch painter Jeronymus Bosch also appear in the animations of Duberg and Berg, all of which have in common the desire to delve deeply into unknown objects and absurd social situations. In particular, the surreal landscapes and bizarre images that could appear in nightmares, which serve as the background for Boss's paintings The Garden of Earthly Delights (1480-90) and Visions of the Afterlife (1505-15), resemble the duo's dreamlike works that encompass the unconscious and irrationality.The animals and moving objects that appear in the work remind us of the fables and fairy tales of La Fontaine, the Brothers Grimm, and Andersen. In these stories, animals resemble humans and refer to allegorical characters or serve as guides to the narrative. Unlike children's stories, which have a strict, linear narrative structure intended to teach moral lessons, the characters and themes float freely in the duo's videos. The story has a circular structure or an ending without a conclusion, and consists of short scenes in which the characters interact through dance or confrontation. The characters move constantly to the music, forming the main narrative flow of the work along with a few fragmentary sentences written in speech bubbles.

If Hans Berg's music is what weaves the characters' stories in a structured way in the video, in the exhibition lighting takes on the role of defining the space, guiding visitors to discover the installations and sculptures for themselves. Lighting in exhibition halls is often considered a difficult task. The stark difference between natural and artificial light, unfounded belief in a perfect light source, and efforts to completely reject reflected light and shadows have erased all the unique characteristics of the exhibition space and made it too bright, making it far from a natural experience. In particular, in exhibitions dominated by video, ‘darkness’ is a dangerous element for visitors, and when it shares space with paintings or sculptures, it is perceived as fatal to the proper appreciation of other works. As a result, the video is often trapped in a ‘non-place’. In other words, in a space where form or characteristics are completely removed, the viewer is naturally erased, and only the experience of being separated from the work and the video and the viewer are essentially separated. However, Duberg and Berg expanded their work into the space itself, where the images can be fully received with a rich sense. In this world of light and shadow, visitors walk through magical paths and fairytale-like pavilions as if traveling.

Pros: Always great exhibitions

Cons: As someone who lives in Gangseo-gu... it's a bit far?

reviews.text:
I only knew about it through Instagram, but I first visited it during the Prime Market! Kim Lia Gallery holds many exhibitions that are particularly pleasing to the eye. It's not an exhibition that feels similar, but there's always something new and changing, so every time I go, I see a good exhibition.
I also have a very fond memory of the time when I asked a question about a work and was given a concise and kind explanation. I'll go see the exhibition again next time :)
